transcript:
Meeting: Quantization technical review - VectorLabs
Date/Time: 2026-04-22 11:00 PT (recorded)
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maia Chen (Redwood SE), Ravi Kumar (Redwood Product), Ethan Cole (VectorLabs ML Eng), Priya Rao (VectorLabs Lead ML), Dana Michaels (VectorLabs Infra), Hector Lin (VectorLabs CTO)

Summary: Quick technical deep dive focused on quantization strategies (INT8 vs FP8 vs GPTQ vs AWQ), expected accuracy regressions, and runtime implications for KV cache / batching / latency on Dedicated vs Private VPC deployments. Action items and next steps agreed to run benchmarks on VectorLabs' prompt set and evaluate model variant tradeoffs.

Topics: quantization options; GPTQ/AWQ accuracy tradeoffs; calibration datasets and outliers; runtime performance (latency/throughput); KV cache interactions; batching strategies; Dedicated vs VPC constraints; security/compliance notes.

--- Transcript ---
00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE, with Maia and Ravi. how's everything on your side?
00:08 Ethan: Hey Jordan, thanks. Ethan here, Priya, Dana, Hector on the call. we've been running into some accuracy drops after we tried int8 on our 13B family, so wanted to understand the tradeoffs and what you recommend.
00:20 Maia: cool, thanks. objective for today is to walk through the quant options and show where we've seen regressions and mitigations. we'll also map that to latency/throughput and KV cache behavior.
00:31 Priya: big thing for us is we need <200ms median token latency on our chat endpoint, and we prefer Dedicated or private VPC. also SOC2 and KMS integration required.
00:44 Jordan: understood. we'll cover that. quick qual: what model family are you using? causal 13B? custom finetune?
00:50 Priya: base is a 13B causal open model with some domain finetune; inference is on our Dedicated GPUs for prod.
00:58 Maia: thanks. ok first, high-level on quant: traditional INT8 (A/B symmetric) reduces memory and usually works well but can incur outlier activation-induced accuracy loss for some instruction tasks. FP8 gives more dynamic range but currently tooling/hardware support varies. GPTQ is per-row/per-channel quantization with calibration that often yields the best accuracy for very low-bit configs, AWQ (almost-weight-quant) is newer and faster to apply with competitive accuracy, esp on causal LLMs.
01:30 Ethan: quick q — what are typical accuracy deltas you see for 13B between FP32 and INT8/GPTQ/AWQ?
01:36 Maia: rough numbers — for 13B on instruction evals: INT8 often has 1-6% drop depending on task and outliers; GPTQ 3-bit can be 0-2% drop if calibrated well; AWQ int4-ish profiles can be within 1-3% in many cases, but it's model dependent. FP8 tends to match FP32 on many tasks if framework and kernels are stable, but FP8 host support is still maturing.
01:58 Priya: ok that's in line with what we saw; our hallucination rate went up on summarization.
02:05 Ravi: one thing to call out — quantization can interact with KV cache and caching logic. when tokens are cached, subsequent calls bypass some compute, but reduced precision can slightly change logits ordering in edge cases which affects beam/ sampling. in practice that's rare but important for deterministic ops.
02:25 Dana: do you see batching causing more regression? we batch a lot to save cost.
02:30 Maia: batching helps throughput but increases tail latency. it also changes per-device memory pressure and can expose quantization-induced numerical instabilities when very large batch sizes cause activation saturation. recommended: configure dynamic batching with small max batch sizes for latency-sensitive routes and preserve a low-latency lane.
02:52 Hector: about Dedicated vs VPC on-prem — any differences in quant kernels? like will AWQ run as well in our private deployment?
02:58 Maia: yes, Redwood's runtime includes kernel selections. AWQ/GPTQ are supported in both Hosted and Dedicated runtimes; on private/on-prem you'll need certain CUDA/toolkit versions. AWQ tends to be faster to compile and lower quant time; GPTQ can be longer to convert (minutes per model). we can share our compile matrix.
03:18 Ethan: can you walk us through the calibration dataset recommendation for GPTQ? we tried a random sample and still saw regressions.
03:25 Maia: GPTQ benefits from representative, diverse calibration data — not just random tokens. include domain-specific prompts and edge-case sequences, ~1k-10k sequences depending on model. also watch for activation outliers — sometimes clipping or per-channel scaling helps.
03:40 Priya: how do you detect activation outliers?
03:42 Maia: runtime stats and profiler. Redwood's optimize toolkit can surface per-layer activation histograms; if a layer has heavy-tail activations, group-wise quantization or per-channel scaling helps. also we sometimes fuse bias/scale tweaks in the quant conversion to reduce mismatch.
03:56 Ethan: latency numbers — what tradeoffs for INT8 vs AWQ vs GPTQ?
04:00 Maia: rough: on same hardware, INT8 kernels can be fastest for pure dense ops because of optimized int GEMMs; AWQ is usually close and often wins in memory-bound cases due to packing; GPTQ inference can be slightly slower if not using fused kernels, but with our runtime optimizations GPTQ inference is within 5-15% of INT8 in many cases. FP8 can be competitive if hardware has native support, but it's less common on older GPUs.
04:28 Dana: for our Dedicated pool (A100s), will AWQ give us immediate memory savings for larger context windows?
04:33 Maia: yes — AWQ/INT8 both reduce model size ~2-4x depending on bitwidth and grouping; that translates to larger effective KV cache capacity or support for longer context windows. one thing: KV cache precision matters — we typically keep KV cache at higher precision or use hybrid strategies: keep activations/kv in FP16 while weights quantized. that reduces regressions.
04:58 Priya: hybrid approach sounds promising. any operational gotchas?
05:02 Maia: complexity of code paths increases; we test fallbacks and dual kernels so rollouts are safe. also quant conversion artifacts can be reproducible across nodes if we pin tool versions.
05:14 Hector: security question — when you do quant conversion or GPTQ pipeline, where does that run and who can access the raw FP32 model?
05:20 Jordan: for Hosted, conversion runs within Redwood environment; we have SOC2 controls, and by default we recommend doing conversions in a customer-controlled environment for sensitive models — Redwood Private supports conversion steps entirely within customer VPC or on-prem. we integrate with KMS for key management.
05:36 Ethan: good. about benchmarks: can you run our prompt set on both AWQ and GPTQ and show accuracy + latency tradeoffs?
05:42 Maia: yes, we can. typical plan: run 1k sample accuracy + latency matrix vs FP32 baseline across top-1/top-3 metrics, plus 95th perc latency. that'll show regressions and tail behavior.
05:54 Jordan: ok onto some deeper details — AWQ internals and group-size effects. AWQ uses per-block quantization with small groups which preserves column distributions; smaller groups -> better accuracy but larger memory and slower kernels. GPTQ tends to do per-row or per-channel corrections during quant step which can yield better low-bit accuracy.
06:18 Priya: do you have automated tooling to pick group size?
06:21 Maia: Redwood Optimize recommends group sizes based on eval regressions; we run a sweep and look at accuracy vs memory curves. often group sizes of 64 or 128 for 8-bit are sweet spots.
06:33 Ravi: another note — when you do quantization in production, keep a canary: route a small fraction of traffic to quantized model and compare signals (QA metrics + drift). Redwood's rollout supports canary + automated rollback if quality degrades.
06:48 Ethan: can you quantify rollback thresholds? like what % drop triggers rollback?
06:52 Jordan: usually customer-defined; we commonly recommend 2-3% relative on key metrics or an absolute increase in error/hallucination rate. we can configure alerts.
07:02 Priya: what about mixed-precision caching — you mentioned storing KV as FP16. does that add network overhead for VPC setups?
07:09 Maia: not really; it's a memory format choice on the worker. if you're distributing KV over network (sharded cache) there could be serialization format concerns, but typically it's in-memory per worker. for VPC you just need the same runtime versions and config.
07:28 Dana: our infra team is concerned about conversion time and impact on deployment windows. GPTQ conversion took hours for our 70B yesterday. any tips?
07:36 Maia: for large models, GPTQ can be slow; AWQ or qLoRA-style post-training quantization is faster. for GPTQ you can parallelize conversion across shards and use lower sample counts for initial tests. also incremental conversion + validation helps.
07:50 Hector: do you see FP8 adoption for production anytime soon?
07:53 Maia: FP8 adoption depends on hardware & driver support; NVIDIA has started enabling FP8 on newer GPUs and frameworks are beginning to expose it. the advantage of FP8 is dynamic range and closer FP32 accuracy, but ecosystem is still catching up.
08:10 Ethan: about accuracy regressions — do you have examples where quantization flips ranking of top tokens and causes catastrophic failure?
08:16 Maia: yes in few edge cases on translation or long-context summarization we've seen token reorderings. mitigation: increased calibration set, per-channel scales, or keeping some layers in higher precision (e.g., first/last 2 layers in FP16). also low-temp sampling can amplify small logit differences.
08:38 Priya: is there tooling to automatically recommend which layers to keep unquantized?
08:42 Maia: Redwood Optimize runs layer-sensitivity analysis and suggests a hybrid quant plan — list of layers that should remain FP16. we surface expected accuracy delta and memory cost.
08:52 Ethan: let's talk numbers — if we do AWQ int4-ish and keep kv in FP16, what latency and cost savings might we expect?
08:59 Maia: sample estimate: for 13B, int4/AWQ could cut model memory ~2.5-3x; cost per token roughly 30-55% reduction depending on batching. latency per token may be neutral or slightly improved if memory-bound; worst-case 10-15% increase if quantized kernels are not fused.
09:20 Dana: we have strict P95 SLO of 400ms. will quantization risk that?
09:24 Maia: depends on batching and tail. plan: run P95 focused benchmarks with your payloads, maintain low-latency lane, and size Dedicated pool for concurrency. Redwood can simulate to find breakpoints.
09:36 Priya: what do you need from us to run the benchmarks?
09:39 Jordan: 200-1,000 sample prompts + golden responses and spec for sampling settings (temp/topk). also indication of target concurrency and batch sizes you plan to use.
09:48 Priya: we'll share 1k prompts and target concurrency: 50 concurrent users, avg request 30 tokens.
09:55 Maia: great. we'll run baseline FP16, INT8, AWQ, and GPTQ variants and return the matrix.
10:03 Ethan: can we also validate hallucination/safety metrics?
10:06 Maia: yes, include checks like factuality scores, overlap with ground truth, and custom heuristics. Redwood's eval harness supports these.
10:12 Jordan: quick note on rollout options: Hosted quickstart then Dedicated pilot then Private conversion in VPC if you want conversion inside your environment.
10:21 Hector: cost: if we move to Dedicated with quantized weights, do we save on reserved capacity needs?
10:26 Jordan: yes, lower memory footprint can reduce node count or allow larger context per node. savings depend on utilization patterns. we'll model it in the spreadsheet.
10:36 Priya: any known bugs or gotchas in Redwood runtime with AWQ?
10:40 Maia: a few early kernel edgecases around fused attention when using specific CUDA drivers — we maintain a compatibility matrix and automated tests; we'll share known issues.
10:50 Dana: on VPC/on-prem, what's the recommended process for key management during conversion?
10:55 Jordan: do conversion entirely within customer network, store models in S3 with customer-managed KMS, and integrate Redwood operator that can pull keys via IAM roles. we support HSM rotations for sensitive customers.
11:06 Priya: good. can you also include a short plan for fallbacks if quant model drifts?
11:10 Maia: yes — rollout with canary, realtime metric compares, automatic traffic shift to FP32/FP16 variant when thresholds trigger, plus manual panic button.
11:18 Jordan: ok time for wrap. recap of next steps...
11:22 Jordan: (recap) Redwood to share: conversion matrix and compatibility doc, quantization comparison spreadsheet with cost/latency/accuracy, and run benchmarks on the 1k prompt set once you share it. VectorLabs to share prompts, define sampling params, and confirm Dedicated pool details.
11:38 Priya: thanks everyone, we'll get the prompts and security contacts over.
11:42 Jordan: great. Maia, Ravi — anything to add?
11:44 Maia: just that we'll include hybrid suggestions (layer keep list) and group-size recommendations.
11:48 Ravi: we'll include cost modeling for Dedicated vs Hosted with quant savings.
11:52 Hector: thanks. that's helpful.
11:55 Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up with docs and the spreadsheet. bye.
